dropped.reason: No solution provided by the school and the question (static versus dynamic equilibrium amounts for a heterogeneous reaction) is ambiguous/flawed, so it cannot be answered reliably

questions.question:
How many position isomers and how many chain isomers does butan-1-ol have?

| | Position isomer | Chain isomer |
|---|---|---|
| (A) | 1 | 1 |
| (B) | 1 | 2 |
| (C) | 2 | 1 |
| (D) | 2 | 2 |
questions.answer: A position isomer keeps the carbon skeleton but moves the functional group: butan-2-ol is the only one (1). Chain isomers have a different carbon skeleton: 2-methylpropan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol (2). Answer B.

questions.question: The structure of a molecule is shown. What is the IUPAC name of the structure?
questions.answer: The longest chain containing the aldehyde carbon has six carbons (hexanal), numbered from the $\text{CHO}$ carbon as C1. This puts the iodine and methyl on C3 and bromine on C5. Substituents are listed alphabetically (bromo, iodo, methyl): 5-bromo-3-iodo-3-methylhexanal. Answer A.

questions.question:
Five structural formulae (I to V) are shown. Which of the following options contains compounds that can form addition polymers?

(A) I and IV

(B) II and III

(C) III and IV

(D) II and V
questions.answer: Addition polymers form from monomers containing a $\text{C=C}$ double bond. Structure II (propene) and V (styrene, phenylethene) both have a $\text{C=C}$ bond. Structure III (a diamine) and IV (ethane-1,2-diol) are condensation monomers, and structure I (bromoethene) is an addition monomer but is paired with the diol in option A. Answer D.

questions.question: A chemist found two unlabelled bottles and deduced that they were propan-1-ol and butan-1-ol. Without the use of reference spectra, which of the following instrumental techniques would be LEAST useful in distinguishing the two compounds?
questions.answer: Both compounds are primary alcohols and both show the same broad $\text{O-H}$ absorption (about $3230$ to $3550\ \text{cm}^{-1}$) and similar $\text{C-H}$ and $\text{C-O}$ absorptions, so infrared cannot easily tell them apart. $^{1}\text{H}$ NMR (number of signals and splitting), $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR (3 versus 4 signals) and mass spectrometry (molecular ion $m/z$ 60 versus 74) all distinguish them. Answer C.

questions.question:
The structures of four organic compounds A to D are shown. Which of the following is most likely to be correct?

(A) Compounds A and C are functional group isomers.

(B) Compound D has a lower melting point than A.

(C) Compound D is more reactive than compound B.

(D) Compound C is less soluble in water than compound A.
questions.answer:
A is pentane, B is pent-1-en-4-yne, C is a chloropentane and D is 2,2-dimethylpropane. A (pentane, $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}$) and C (a chloroalkane) have different molecular formulas so cannot be isomers (A is false). Compound B has $\text{C=C}$ and $\text{C}\equiv\text{C}$ bonds and is more reactive than saturated D (C is false). The polar $\text{C-Cl}$ bond makes C at least as soluble in water as pentane, so D is not correct. By elimination the intended answer is B.

*Note: the school's explanation (D is more compact so packs better) would actually imply a higher melting point for D, and real data have neopentane melting higher than pentane. B is nonetheless the intended best option; the school's reasoning is the wrong way round.*
options: Compounds A and C are functional group isomers.
Compound D has a lower melting point than A.
Compound D is more reactive than compound B.
Compound C is less soluble in water than compound A.

questions.question:
The $K_a$ values of some weak acids are:

| Acid | $K_a$ |
|---|---|
| HOBr | $2.3 \times 10^{-9}$ |
| HOCl | $3.5 \times 10^{-8}$ |
| HF | $7.2 \times 10^{-4}$ |
| HCOOH | $1.8 \times 10^{-4}$ |

Which of the following acids would produce the strongest conjugate base?
questions.answer: The weaker the acid (the smaller $K_a$), the stronger its conjugate base. HOBr has the smallest $K_a$ ($2.3\times10^{-9}$), so $\text{OBr}^-$ is the strongest conjugate base. Answer A.

questions.question: Which of the following changes takes place when $500\ \text{mL}$ of water is added to $500\ \text{mL}$ of $1.00\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ acetic acid?
questions.answer: Dilution reduces $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$, so the pH increases. By Le Chatelier's principle (or the dilution law for a weak acid) the equilibrium $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}+\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ shifts towards more particles, so a larger fraction of the acid ionises and the percentage ionisation increases. Answer A.
options: pH increases and percentage ionisation increases.
pH increases and percentage ionisation does not change.
pH decreases and percentage ionisation does not change.
pH decreases and percentage ionisation decreases.

questions.question: A spirit burner used $26.6\ \text{g}$ of ethanol to heat $1.00\ \text{L}$ of water from $23.5\ ^\circ\text{C}$ to $100.0\ ^\circ\text{C}$. The molar heat of combustion of ethanol is $1367\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. What percentage of the heat produced by the burner was lost to the environment?
questions.answer:
$q = mc\Delta T = 1000 \times 4.18 \times (100.0-23.5) = 3.198\times10^{5}\ \text{J} = 319.8\ \text{kJ}$ absorbed by the water.

$n(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}) = \dfrac{26.6}{46.07} = 0.5774\ \text{mol}$, so heat released $= 0.5774 \times 1367 = 789.3\ \text{kJ}$.

Percentage absorbed $= \dfrac{319.8}{789.3}\times 100 = 40.5\%$, so the percentage lost is $100 - 40.5 = 59.5\%$. Answer C.

questions.question: The reaction $\text{CO}(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}_2(g) + \text{H}_2(g)$, $\Delta H = -41\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, is used to produce hydrogen gas. It is carried out in a sealed container with a catalyst (dashed line) and without a catalyst (solid line), all other conditions unchanged. Which graph shows the change in hydrogen gas concentration with time for the uncatalysed and catalysed reactions?
questions.answer: A catalyst lowers the activation energy for both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner (steeper initial rise for the dashed line) but the equilibrium position, and hence the final $[\text{H}_2]$, is unchanged. Only graph A has the catalysed (dashed) curve rising faster to the same final concentration. Answer A.

questions.question: The equilibrium $\text{Fe}^{3+}(aq)\ (\text{yellow}) + \text{SCN}^-(aq)\ (\text{colourless}) \rightleftharpoons \text{Fe(SCN)}^{2+}(aq)\ (\text{red})$ is established in an iron(III) chloride / potassium thiocyanate mixture. Which graph best represents the changes in concentration when water is added to the equilibrium mixture at time $t_2$?
questions.answer: Adding water dilutes every species, so all three concentrations drop instantly at $t_2$. The system then shifts to the side with more dissolved particles (left, 2 particles versus 1), so $[\text{Fe}^{3+}]$ and $[\text{SCN}^-]$ partly recover while $[\text{Fe(SCN)}^{2+}]$ falls further before levelling out. Only graph B shows this. Answer B.

questions.question:
The graph shows the titration curve for a particular acid and a particular base. Which indicator would be best suited to this titration?

| | Indicator | Colour change range (pH) |
|---|---|---|
| (A) | Bromophenol blue | 6.2 - 7.6 |
| (B) | Magdala red | 3.0 - 4.0 |
| (C) | Phenolphthalein | 8.2 - 10.0 |
| (D) | Chlorophenol red | 5.2 - 6.8 |
questions.answer: The curve starts at about pH 3 and has a buffer region at pH 4 to 5, so the acid is weak and the base is strong. The vertical section (equivalence point at $25\ \text{mL}$) rises from about pH 7 to 11, and the equivalence point is above pH 7 (about pH 8.5 to 9) because the conjugate base of the weak acid is present. The indicator's range should lie within the steep section at the equivalence point, which is phenolphthalein (8.2 - 10.0). Answer C.

questions.question:
The same titration curve (a weak acid with a strong base, starting near pH 3 and with a buffer region around pH 4 to 5) is shown. The buffer region for this titration curve may contain:

(A) NaCl and NaOH

(B) $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$

(C) $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$

(D) $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{COONH}_4$
questions.answer: A buffer is a weak acid with its conjugate base. The curve starts at about pH 3 and levels off in a buffer region of pH 4 to 5, so it is a weak acid titrated with a strong base; $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}/\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$ (pH about 4.7) fits. $\text{NH}_3/\text{NH}_4^+$ buffers at about pH 9, $\text{NaCl}/\text{NaOH}$ is not a buffer. Answer B.

questions.question:
The graph shows the percentage of gaseous products at equilibrium against pressure at two temperatures, $T\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and $(T+10)\ ^\circ\text{C}$, for a reversible reaction. Which reaction could be represented?

(A) $\text{N}_2(g)+3\text{H}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g)$, $\Delta H=-92\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$

(B) $3\text{O}_2(g)+4\text{NH}_3(g)\rightleftharpoons 2\text{N}_2(g)+6\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)$, $\Delta H=-1248\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$

(C) $2\text{N}_2(g)+\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons 2\text{N}_2\text{O}(g)$, $\Delta H=+82\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$

(D) $\text{CO}_2(g)+\text{C}(s)\rightleftharpoons 2\text{CO}(g)$, $\Delta H=+173\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$
questions.answer: The higher temperature gives a greater percentage of products, so the forward reaction is endothermic ($\Delta H>0$); this rules out A and B. The percentage of products falls as pressure increases, so the equilibrium shifts towards the side with fewer moles of gas, meaning the products side has more gas moles than the reactants. In C the products side has fewer gas moles (2 versus 3), so higher pressure would increase the product percentage. In D there are 2 mol of gas on the products side and 1 mol on the reactants side, which fits. Answer D.

questions.question: Colourless nitrous oxide ($\text{N}_2\text{O}$) reacts with oxygen to form brown nitrogen dioxide: $2\text{N}_2\text{O}(g)+3\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons 4\text{NO}_2(g)$, $\Delta H=-32\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. $0.27\ \text{mol}$ of $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ was placed in a $4.00\ \text{L}$ vessel with $0.42\ \text{mol}$ of oxygen. At equilibrium $0.15\ \text{mol}$ of $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ remained. Calculate a value for the equilibrium constant at the given temperature.
questions.answer:
$\text{N}_2\text{O}$ reacted $= 0.27-0.15 = 0.12\ \text{mol}$, so $\text{O}_2$ reacted $= \tfrac{3}{2}(0.12)=0.18\ \text{mol}$ and $\text{NO}_2$ formed $= 2(0.12)=0.24\ \text{mol}$.

At equilibrium: $n(\text{N}_2\text{O})=0.15$, $n(\text{O}_2)=0.42-0.18=0.24$, $n(\text{NO}_2)=0.24\ \text{mol}$. Concentrations (divide by $4.00\ \text{L}$): $0.0375$, $0.060$, $0.060\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

$$K = \frac{[\text{NO}_2]^4}{[\text{N}_2\text{O}]^2[\text{O}_2]^3} = \frac{(0.060)^4}{(0.0375)^2(0.060)^3} = 42.67$$

Answer C.

questions.question:
In a titration of a strong base with strong acid, the following procedure was used:

1. A burette was rinsed with water and then filled with the standard acid.
2. A pipette was rinsed with some base solution.
3. A conical flask was rinsed with some base solution.
4. A pipette was used to transfer a measured volume of base solution into the conical flask.
5. Indicator was added to the base solution, and it was titrated to the endpoint with the acid.

Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.answer: Rinsing the burette with water leaves water that dilutes the standard acid, so a larger titre is needed. Rinsing the conical flask with base solution leaves extra base in the flask (beyond the pipetted volume), which also needs extra acid. (Rinsing the pipette with base is correct.) Both errors increase the titre, so the calculated base concentration is too high. Answer C.
options: The calculated base concentration will be lower than the actual base concentration.
The calculated base concentration will be the same as the actual base concentration.
The calculated base concentration will be higher than the actual base concentration.
No definite conclusion can be drawn about the calculated base concentration.

questions.question: The $K_{sp}$ of strontium hydroxide is $2.0\times10^{-3}$. What is the pH of a saturated solution of strontium hydroxide?
questions.answer:
$\text{Sr(OH)}_2(s)\rightleftharpoons \text{Sr}^{2+}(aq)+2\text{OH}^-(aq)$. If the solubility is $x$, $K_{sp}=x(2x)^2=4x^3=2.0\times10^{-3}$, so $x=\sqrt[3]{5.0\times10^{-4}}=0.0794\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

$[\text{OH}^-]=2x=0.159\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$, $\text{pOH}=-\log_{10}(0.159)=0.80$, so $\text{pH}=14-0.80=13.20$. Answer D.

questions.question: A $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR spectrum is shown (peaks at about 151, 108, 35, 22 and 21 ppm). Which compound gives rise to this spectrum?
questions.answer: The spectrum has five peaks, so the molecule has five carbon environments (and alkene carbons at about 108 and 151 ppm). Hex-1-ene has 6 environments, 2-methylpent-2-ene has 6, and 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene (symmetrical) has only 2. 2,3-dimethylbut-1-ene, $\text{CH}_2{=}\text{C(CH}_3)\text{CH(CH}_3)_2$, has 5: $=\text{CH}_2$, $=\text{C}<$, $\text{CH}$, the $\text{CH}_3$ on the alkene carbon, and the two equivalent $\text{CH}_3$ groups of the isopropyl group. Answer C.

questions.question:
An analytical chemist tested a compound X and obtained these results.

| Analysis | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Infrared spectroscopy | Broad absorption at $3385\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ |
| Percentage composition by mass | C = 70.53%, H = 13.81%, O = 15.66% |
| Mass spectrometry | Molecular ion peak: $m/z = 102$ |
| Test with acidified potassium dichromate | Orange colour remains on heating X with acidified potassium dichromate in a water bath |

Which of the following is a possible structure for compound X?
questions.answer:
The broad band at $3385\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ indicates an $\text{O-H}$ group in an alcohol, and no colour change with dichromate shows it is not a primary or secondary alcohol (so a tertiary alcohol). This rules out hexan-1-ol (primary) and 2-methylpentan-3-ol (secondary). Moles: C $70.53/12.01=5.87$, H $13.81/1.008=13.70$, O $15.66/16.00=0.979$, ratio $6:14:1$, empirical formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}\text{O}$ ($M=102$), which does not match 3-methylbutanoic acid ($\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_2$). The answer is the tertiary alcohol 3-methylpentan-3-ol. Answer D.

*Note: the school's marker notes print the empirical formula as $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{14}\text{O}$ in one place; the correct ratio from their own table is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}\text{O}$.*

questions.question: A sample of 1,2,3,4-tetrachlorobutane was analysed using a mass spectrometer. The only isotopes present in the compound are hydrogen-1, carbon-12, chlorine-35 and chlorine-37. Determine the number of molecular ion peaks in the mass spectrum of 1,2,3,4-tetrachlorobutane.
questions.answer: The molecule contains four chlorine atoms, each either $^{35}\text{Cl}$ or $^{37}\text{Cl}$. The number of $^{37}\text{Cl}$ atoms can be 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4, giving molecular ions of $m/z$ 194, 196, 198, 200 and 202: five peaks. Answer D.

questions.question: Methane and steam react to form carbon monoxide and hydrogen according to the equation $\text{CH}_4(g)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)\rightleftharpoons \text{CO}(g)+3\text{H}_2(g)$, $\Delta H=+131\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. $4.0\ \text{mol}$ of methane and $5.0\ \text{mol}$ of steam are placed in a sealed $2.0\ \text{L}$ container, heated to $450\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and allowed to reach equilibrium. At equilibrium there are $1.5\ \text{mol}$ of methane in the container. Determine the number of moles of the other gases at equilibrium.
questions.answer:
| | $\text{CH}_4$ | $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ | $\text{CO}$ | $\text{H}_2$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Initial (mol) | 4.0 | 5.0 | 0 | 0 |
| Change (mol) | $-2.5$ | $-2.5$ | $+2.5$ | $+7.5$ |
| Equilibrium (mol) | 1.5 | 2.5 | 2.5 | 7.5 |

$\text{CH}_4$ decreases by $4.0-1.5=2.5\ \text{mol}$, so by the 1:1:1:3 ratio $n(\text{H}_2\text{O})=2.5\ \text{mol}$, $n(\text{CO})=2.5\ \text{mol}$ and $n(\text{H}_2)=3\times2.5=7.5\ \text{mol}$.

questions.question: Methane and steam react according to $\text{CH}_4(g)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)\rightleftharpoons \text{CO}(g)+3\text{H}_2(g)$, $\Delta H=+131\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Write the expression for the equilibrium constant for this reaction.
questions.answer: $$K_{eq}=\frac{[\text{CO}][\text{H}_2]^3}{[\text{CH}_4][\text{H}_2\text{O}]}$$

questions.question: Methane and steam react to form carbon monoxide and hydrogen according to the equation $\text{CH}_4(g)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)\rightleftharpoons \text{CO}(g)+3\text{H}_2(g)$, $\Delta H=+131\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. $4.0\ \text{mol}$ of methane and $5.0\ \text{mol}$ of steam are placed in a sealed $2.0\ \text{L}$ container, heated to $450\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and allowed to reach equilibrium. At equilibrium there are $1.5\ \text{mol}$ of methane in the container. The equilibrium amounts are $1.5\ \text{mol}\ \text{CH}_4$, $2.5\ \text{mol}\ \text{H}_2\text{O}$, $2.5\ \text{mol}\ \text{CO}$ and $7.5\ \text{mol}\ \text{H}_2$. Determine the numerical value of the equilibrium constant at $450\ ^\circ\text{C}$.
questions.answer:
Concentrations (volume $2.0\ \text{L}$): $[\text{CH}_4]=0.75$, $[\text{H}_2\text{O}]=1.25$, $[\text{CO}]=1.25$, $[\text{H}_2]=3.75\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

$$K_{eq}=\frac{[\text{CO}][\text{H}_2]^3}{[\text{CH}_4][\text{H}_2\text{O}]}=\frac{(1.25)(3.75)^3}{(0.75)(1.25)}=\frac{(3.75)^3}{0.75}=70.3\ (\approx 70)$$

*Note: the school's criteria print 70.13; the correct calculation gives 70.3 (they accept 70).*

questions.question: Swimming pool water should be nearly neutral, close to pH 7. The indicator chart shows the colour ranges of methyl orange, bromothymol blue and phenolphthalein. With reference to each of the indicators in the chart, explain which indicator(s) would be best suited to determine the safety of the pool water.
questions.answer:
**Bromothymol blue** is the best choice. It changes colour (yellow to blue, passing through green) over about pH 6.0 to 7.6, so pH 7 lies inside its range and a green colour shows the water is close to neutral, while yellow or blue shows it is too acidic or too basic.

**Methyl orange** changes colour at about pH 3 to 4.5 (red to yellow), so it is already yellow at pH 7 and stays yellow in all basic solutions; it cannot show whether the pool is neutral or too basic.

**Phenolphthalein** changes colour at about pH 8.2 to 10 (colourless to pink), so it is colourless at pH 7 and in all acidic solutions; it cannot show whether the pool is neutral or too acidic.

questions.question: Calculate the pH of the resulting solution when $25.0\ \text{mL}$ of $0.010\ \text{M}$ KOH is mixed with $50.0\ \text{mL}$ of $0.20\ \text{M}$ $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, assuming that sulfuric acid undergoes complete ionisation.
questions.answer:
$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq)+2\text{KOH}(aq)\rightarrow \text{K}_2\text{SO}_4(aq)+2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$

$n(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4)=0.20\times0.0500=0.010\ \text{mol}$; $n(\text{KOH})=0.010\times0.0250=2.5\times10^{-4}\ \text{mol}$.

$\text{KOH}$ is limiting: it uses $\tfrac12(2.5\times10^{-4})=1.25\times10^{-4}\ \text{mol}$ of $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$. Excess $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4=0.010-1.25\times10^{-4}=9.875\times10^{-3}\ \text{mol}$.

Complete ionisation gives $n(\text{H}^+)=2\times9.875\times10^{-3}=0.01975\ \text{mol}$ in a total volume of $0.0750\ \text{L}$.

$[\text{H}^+]=\dfrac{0.01975}{0.0750}=0.2633\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$, so $\text{pH}=-\log_{10}(0.2633)=0.58$.

questions.question: Explain the use of $\text{KH}_2\text{PO}_4$ to neutralise strong acid and strong base spills with reference to its chemical properties. Support your answer with relevant equations.
questions.answer:
$\text{KH}_2\text{PO}_4$ dissolves to give $\text{K}^+$ and $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$: $\text{KH}_2\text{PO}_4(aq)\rightarrow \text{K}^+(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-(aq)$.

$\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ is **amphiprotic**: it can donate a proton (Brønsted-Lowry acid) or accept a proton (Brønsted-Lowry base), so it can neutralise both types of spill.

*Strong acid spill:* the $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ acts as a base (proton acceptor) and removes the $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$:
$$\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)\rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
$\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ is a weak acid, so the spill is neutralised to a much safer, less acidic solution.

*Strong base spill:* the $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ acts as an acid (proton donor) and removes the $\text{OH}^-$:
$$\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-(aq)+\text{OH}^-(aq)\rightarrow \text{HPO}_4^{2-}(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
$\text{HPO}_4^{2-}$ is only a weak base, so the strongly basic solution is neutralised to a safer one.

questions.question: In an experiment to demonstrate diffusion of gases, plugs of cotton wool soaked in concentrated hydrochloric acid and concentrated ammonia are placed at opposite ends of a horizontal glass tube. After a few minutes a white ring forms in the tube, closer to the end with the hydrochloric acid. Write a balanced chemical equation for the reaction that occurs and assess the suitability of Arrhenius' theory to classify it as an acid-base reaction.
questions.answer:
$$\text{HCl}(g)+\text{NH}_3(g)\rightarrow \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}(s)$$

Arrhenius' theory defines acids as substances that release $\text{H}^+$ ions in aqueous solution and bases as substances that release $\text{OH}^-$ ions in aqueous solution. This reaction occurs between gaseous molecules in the air inside the tube, with no water (aqueous solution) present, and ammonia does not contain or release $\text{OH}^-$. Arrhenius' theory is therefore not suitable to classify it as an acid-base reaction (the Brønsted-Lowry theory, with $\text{HCl}$ donating a proton to $\text{NH}_3$, is).

questions.question: In a pickling process, rust (iron(III) oxide, $\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$) is dissolved by pickling liquor containing hydrochloric acid. Iron(III) oxide is a base, insoluble in water but highly soluble in HCl: $\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3(s)+6\text{HCl}(aq)\rightarrow 2\text{FeCl}_3(aq)+3\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$. State whether iron(III) oxide can be classified as a Brønsted-Lowry acid/base or an Arrhenius acid/base. Justify your response.
questions.answer:
Iron(III) oxide is a **Brønsted-Lowry base** but not an Arrhenius base.

The Arrhenius theory defines a base as a substance that releases $\text{OH}^-$ ions in water. $\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$ is insoluble in water and is composed of $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ and $\text{O}^{2-}$ ions; it does not dissociate to release $\text{OH}^-$, so it does not fit the Arrhenius definition, which is limited to substances that give $\text{OH}^-$ in solution.

The Brønsted-Lowry theory defines acids as proton donors and bases as proton acceptors. In the reaction, $\text{HCl}$ (ionised as $\text{H}^+$/$\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) donates protons, so it is the acid. The oxide ion $\text{O}^{2-}$ in $\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$ accepts two protons to form $\text{H}_2\text{O}$:
$$\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3(s)+6\text{H}^+(aq)\rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{3+}(aq)+3\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
Since $\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$ accepts protons, it is a Brønsted-Lowry base. The Brønsted-Lowry theory therefore explains the basic behaviour of iron(III) oxide, even though it is insoluble and releases no $\text{OH}^-$.

questions.question: A $25.0\ \text{mL}$ sample of $0.120\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ ammonium hydroxide solution was titrated against nitric acid from an unlabelled bottle. The titres were: 1: $18.2\ \text{mL}$, 2: $18.1\ \text{mL}$, 3: $21.4\ \text{mL}$, 4: $18.1\ \text{mL}$. Calculate the concentration of the nitric acid solution.
questions.answer:
$\text{NH}_4\text{OH}(aq)+\text{HNO}_3(aq)\rightarrow \text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$ (1:1 ratio)

Titre 3 ($21.4\ \text{mL}$) is not concordant and is discarded. Average titre $=\dfrac{18.2+18.1+18.1}{3}=18.13\ \text{mL}=0.01813\ \text{L}$.

$n(\text{NH}_4\text{OH})=0.120\times0.0250=3.00\times10^{-3}\ \text{mol}=n(\text{HNO}_3)$.

$$c(\text{HNO}_3)=\frac{3.00\times10^{-3}}{0.01813}=0.165\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

questions.question: Ammonium hydroxide solution was titrated with nitric acid, producing a solution of ammonium nitrate, $\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3$. Using a chemical equation, explain the pH of the resultant salt solution.
questions.answer:
$\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3$ dissociates completely: $\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3(aq)\rightarrow \text{NH}_4^+(aq)+\text{NO}_3^-(aq)$.

$\text{NO}_3^-$ is the conjugate base of the strong acid $\text{HNO}_3$, so it is too weak a base to react with water (it is a neutral spectator). $\text{NH}_4^+$ is the conjugate acid of the weak base $\text{NH}_3$ and undergoes hydrolysis, donating a proton to water:
$$\text{NH}_4^+(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_3(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$$
This produces $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$, so the salt solution is acidic and its pH is less than 7.

questions.question: A manufacturer from the Hunter region claims its red wine has an alcohol content of $40.0\%\ (\text{v/v})$. A $50.00\ \text{mL}$ sample of the wine is transferred to a $500.0\ \text{mL}$ volumetric flask and made up to the mark with water. A $20.00\ \text{mL}$ aliquot is titrated with $0.5022\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ $\text{KMnO}_4$ (appropriate indicator added). The reaction is $4\text{MnO}_4^-(aq)+5\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}(aq)+12\text{H}^+(aq)\rightarrow 4\text{Mn}^{2+}(aq)+5\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}(aq)+11\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$. The $\text{MnO}_4^-$ ion is intensely purple and $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ is colourless. The average of the concordant titres is $23.22\ \text{mL}$. The density of ethanol is $0.789\ \text{g mL}^{-1}$. Calculate the concentration of ethanol in $\%\ (\text{v/v})$ in the red wine that Bobby titrated.
questions.answer:
$n(\text{MnO}_4^-)=0.5022\times0.02322=1.1661\times10^{-2}\ \text{mol}$

$n(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH})=1.1661\times10^{-2}\times\tfrac54=1.4576\times10^{-2}\ \text{mol}$ in the $20.00\ \text{mL}$ aliquot.

Diluted concentration $=\dfrac{1.4576\times10^{-2}}{0.02000}=0.7288\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$. The wine was diluted $50\to500\ \text{mL}$ (factor 10), so the original concentration is $7.288\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

Mass per litre $=7.288\times46.068=335.7\ \text{g L}^{-1}$. Volume of ethanol per litre $=\dfrac{335.7}{0.789}=425.5\ \text{mL}$ in $1000\ \text{mL}$.

$$\%\ (\text{v/v})=\frac{425.5}{1000}\times100=42.6\%$$

questions.question: A manufacturer from the Hunter region claims its red wine has an alcohol content of $40.0\%\ (\text{v/v})$. A $50.00\ \text{mL}$ sample of the wine is transferred to a $500.0\ \text{mL}$ volumetric flask and made up to the mark with water. A $20.00\ \text{mL}$ aliquot is titrated with $0.5022\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ $\text{KMnO}_4$ (appropriate indicator added). The reaction is $4\text{MnO}_4^-(aq)+5\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}(aq)+12\text{H}^+(aq)\rightarrow 4\text{Mn}^{2+}(aq)+5\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}(aq)+11\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$. The $\text{MnO}_4^-$ ion is intensely purple and $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ is colourless. The average of the concordant titres is $23.22\ \text{mL}$. Bobby found that $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ can act as a catalyst for the reduction of $\text{MnO}_4^-$, and that a brown solid, most likely $\text{MnO}_2$, forms during the titration from the incomplete reduction of $\text{MnO}_4^-$, so these $\text{MnO}_4^-$ ions oxidise a smaller amount of ethanol. The titration gave $42.6\%\ (\text{v/v})$. Using this information, assess the manufacturer's claim of $40.0\%\ (\text{v/v})$.
questions.answer:
When some $\text{MnO}_4^-$ is reduced only to brown $\text{MnO}_2$ (a 3-electron reduction instead of 5), each $\text{MnO}_4^-$ oxidises less ethanol than the equation assumes. More $\text{KMnO}_4$ solution (a larger titre) is therefore needed to oxidise all the ethanol, and the calculated ethanol content ($42.6\%$) is higher than the true ethanol content.

Because the true value is lower than $42.6\%$, it could well be $40.0\%$. The experiment therefore does not show that the manufacturer's claim is false: the claim could be correct, but the result alone cannot confirm it either (the size of the error is unknown). *(Answers may vary, but the justification must support the claim made.)*

questions.question:
$50\ \text{mL}$ of $0.10\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ strong acid HZ was titrated with $0.10\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ strong base MOH while the pH was measured. Show relevant calculations and complete the missing pH values in the table.

| # | Volume of MOH added (mL) | pH |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 1.0 |
| 2 | 25 | |
| 3 | 49 | |
| 4 | 50 | 7.0 |
| 5 | 51 | |
| 6 | 75 | 12.3 |
questions.answer:
$\text{HZ}+\text{MOH}\rightarrow \text{MZ}+\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (1:1). $n(\text{HZ})_{initial}=0.10\times0.050=5.0\times10^{-3}\ \text{mol}$.

**#2 (25 mL):** $n(\text{MOH})=0.10\times0.025=2.5\times10^{-3}\ \text{mol}$; $n(\text{H}^+)$ left $=2.5\times10^{-3}\ \text{mol}$ in $0.075\ \text{L}$: $[\text{H}^+]=0.0333$, $\text{pH}=1.5$.

**#3 (49 mL):** $n(\text{MOH})=4.9\times10^{-3}$; $n(\text{H}^+)$ left $=1.0\times10^{-4}\ \text{mol}$ in $0.099\ \text{L}$: $[\text{H}^+]=1.01\times10^{-3}$, $\text{pH}=3.0$.

**#5 (51 mL):** $n(\text{OH}^-)$ in excess $=0.10\times0.051-5.0\times10^{-3}=1.0\times10^{-4}\ \text{mol}$ in $0.101\ \text{L}$: $[\text{OH}^-]=9.9\times10^{-4}$, $\text{pOH}=3.0$, $\text{pH}=11.0$.

Completed table: #2 = 1.5, #3 = 3.0, #5 = 11.0.

questions.question:
A titration of $50\ \text{mL}$ of $0.10\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ strong acid HZ with $0.10\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ strong base MOH gave these pH values.

| Volume of MOH added (mL) | 0 | 25 | 49 | 50 | 51 | 75 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| pH | 1.0 | 1.5 | 3.0 | 7.0 | 11.0 | 12.3 |

Draw an appropriately labelled titration curve using the data and identify any TWO key characteristics of the curve.
questions.answer:
The titration curve (pH on the vertical axis against volume of MOH added) is shown below: a slow rise from pH 1, a near-vertical section between about 49 and 51 mL, then a slow rise towards about pH 12 to 13.

Key characteristics (any two):
- The initial pH is 1 because the strong acid is fully ionised ($[\text{H}^+]=0.10\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$).
- The equivalence point is at $50\ \text{mL}$ where $n(\text{H}^+)=n(\text{OH}^-)$, at pH 7.0 because the salt formed from a strong acid and strong base is neutral.
- The pH changes very rapidly (a vertical section from about pH 3 to 11) near the equivalence point, so many indicators would be suitable.
- There is no buffer region (the curve has no flat section at moderate pH values), since both acid and base are strong.
- After the equivalence point the pH levels off at a high value, determined by the excess $\text{OH}^-$.

questions.question:
An industrial process for a chemical used in fertilisers is represented by $4\text{R}(g)\rightleftharpoons 2\text{P}(g)$, $\Delta H<0$ (optimal at $500\ ^\circ\text{C}$). All reactants are added to chamber 1 at $100\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and $200\ \text{atm}$ and allowed to reach equilibrium. After 4 hours the gas mixture is moved to a larger chamber 2 ($100\ ^\circ\text{C}$) and passed over several layers of catalyst. After 8 hours it is moved to chamber 3 (same catalyst layers) but the temperature is raised to $500\ ^\circ\text{C}$. After 12 hours the mixture goes to chamber 4 for purification.

Sketch a graph of rate of reaction against time (0 to 12 hours), showing the rates of the forward reaction (solid line) and the backward reaction (dashed line) in each chamber.
questions.answer:
Key features of the sketch (see graph):
- **Chamber 1 (0-4 h):** the forward rate starts high (only reactants present) and falls as reactant is used; the backward rate starts at zero and rises as product forms. The two meet at a constant, equal, non-zero rate when equilibrium is reached (before 4 h); this rate (ROR$_1$) is low because of the low temperature.
- **Chamber 2 (4-8 h):** the catalyst increases the forward and backward rates by the same amount, so they step up together to a higher equal value (ROR$_2 >$ ROR$_1$) and stay equal (still at equilibrium; marker accepts a straight line since the chamber volume is not to scale).
- **Chamber 3 (8-12 h):** the higher temperature increases both rates sharply, but the backward (endothermic) rate increases more, so it jumps above the forward rate; then the forward rate rises and the backward rate falls until they are equal again at a new constant value, ROR$_3>$ ROR$_2$.

questions.question:
An industrial process for a chemical used in fertilisers is represented by $4\text{R}(g)\rightleftharpoons 2\text{P}(g)$, $\Delta H<0$ (optimal at $500\ ^\circ\text{C}$). All reactants are added to chamber 1 at $100\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and $200\ \text{atm}$ and allowed to reach equilibrium. After 4 hours the gas mixture is moved to a larger chamber 2 ($100\ ^\circ\text{C}$) and passed over several layers of catalyst. After 8 hours it is moved to chamber 3 (same catalyst layers) at $500\ ^\circ\text{C}$.

Using collision theory and Le Chatelier's principle, explain the changes in the rate of reaction and the concentration of the reaction mixture in chambers 1, 2 and 3 only.
questions.answer:
**Chamber 1 ($100\ ^\circ\text{C}$, $200\ \text{atm}$).** Initially only R is present, so the forward rate is highest because the high concentration gives frequent collisions; the backward rate is zero. As R is consumed the forward rate falls (fewer collisions), and as P builds up the backward rate rises. When the rates are equal the system is at dynamic equilibrium and the concentrations of R and P are constant. The rates are low because at $100\ ^\circ\text{C}$ few particles have energy at least the activation energy, so few collisions are successful.

**Chamber 2 ($100\ ^\circ\text{C}$, larger volume, catalyst).** The volume increases, so the pressure drops (from $PV=nRT$) and all concentrations fall. By Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts to the side with more gas moles (left, 4 mol versus 2 mol) to oppose the pressure decrease, so $[\text{R}]$ partly recovers and $[\text{P}]$ falls further; both rates decrease slightly from this effect. The catalyst provides an alternative pathway of lower activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful and both the forward and backward rates increase equally; the catalyst does not change the equilibrium position but the new equilibrium is established faster. Overall the rate is higher than in chamber 1.

**Chamber 3 ($500\ ^\circ\text{C}$, catalyst).** The temperature increase means more particles have energy greater than the activation energy and collisions are more frequent, so both rates increase a lot (the rate is highest here). The forward reaction is exothermic, so the equilibrium shifts left (the endothermic direction) to absorb the added heat; the backward rate increases more than the forward rate at first, $[\text{P}]$ decreases and $[\text{R}]$ increases until the rates are again equal at the new, higher value and the concentrations are constant again (after 8 hours the system stays at $500\ ^\circ\text{C}$ until 12 hours).

questions.question:
$\text{H}_3\text{AsO}_4$ is a weak triprotic acid that releases its hydrogen ions in three steps:

Step 1: $\text{H}_3\text{AsO}_4(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{AsO}_4^-(aq)$, $pK_{a1}=2.24$

Step 2: $\text{H}_2\text{AsO}_4^-(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)+\text{HAsO}_4^{2-}(aq)$, $pK_{a2}=6.96$

Step 3: $\text{HAsO}_4^{2-}(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)+\text{AsO}_4^{3-}(aq)$, $pK_{a3}=11.50$

Derive the expression for the equilibrium constant ($K_{eq}$) for the reaction $\text{H}_3\text{AsO}_4(aq)+3\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons 3\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)+\text{AsO}_4^{3-}(aq)$ and calculate its value.
questions.answer:
The overall reaction is the sum of steps 1, 2 and 3, so
$$K_{eq}=\frac{[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]^3[\text{AsO}_4^{3-}]}{[\text{H}_3\text{AsO}_4]}$$
Proof: $K_{a1}\times K_{a2}\times K_{a3}=\dfrac{[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+][\text{H}_2\text{AsO}_4^-]}{[\text{H}_3\text{AsO}_4]}\times\dfrac{[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+][\text{HAsO}_4^{2-}]}{[\text{H}_2\text{AsO}_4^-]}\times\dfrac{[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+][\text{AsO}_4^{3-}]}{[\text{HAsO}_4^{2-}]}=\dfrac{[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]^3[\text{AsO}_4^{3-}]}{[\text{H}_3\text{AsO}_4]}=K_{eq}$ (the intermediates cancel).

$K_{a1}=10^{-2.24}=5.75\times10^{-3}$, $K_{a2}=10^{-6.96}=1.10\times10^{-7}$, $K_{a3}=10^{-11.50}=3.16\times10^{-12}$.

$$K_{eq}=(5.75\times10^{-3})(1.10\times10^{-7})(3.16\times10^{-12})=2.00\times10^{-21}$$
(equivalently $10^{-(2.24+6.96+11.50)}=10^{-20.70}$.)

questions.question: James placed $100\ \text{g}$ of glucose ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$) into a conical flask, dissolved it in water and added yeast. He weighed the flask with its contents, warmed it to $32\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and left it for about 2 days until the reaction was complete. Initial mass of conical flask with mixture $=335.2\ \text{g}$; final mass $=319.4\ \text{g}$. Calculate the mass of glucose consumed in the reaction.
questions.answer:
Fermentation: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6(aq)\rightarrow 2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}(aq)+2\text{CO}_2(g)$

The mass lost is the $\text{CO}_2$ that escaped: $m(\text{CO}_2)=335.2-319.4=15.8\ \text{g}$.

$n(\text{CO}_2)=\dfrac{15.8}{44.01}=0.3590\ \text{mol}$.

$n(\text{glucose})=\tfrac12\times0.3590=0.1795\ \text{mol}$.

$m(\text{glucose})=0.1795\times180.16=32.3\ \text{g}$.

questions.question:
Charlie made methyl salicylate (a minty-smelling ester) using this method:

1. Dissolve $3.0\ \text{g}$ of salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid) in $20\ \text{mL}$ of methanol in a conical flask.
2. Add $1\ \text{mL}$ of concentrated sulfuric acid and place the flask in a hot water bath set up above a Bunsen burner.
3. Monitor the flask by continuously moving it out of the water bath when it is close to boiling, then moving it back in to heat the mixture again.
4. Remove the flask from the water bath after 10 minutes.
5. Add dilute sodium carbonate solution and swirl until the mixture stops reacting.
6. Pour the reaction mixture into a separating funnel and wait until two layers form.
7. Discard the bottom layer and keep the top layer as the product, methyl salicylate.

Suggest modifications that could be made to the procedure to improve the production and extraction of pure methyl salicylate. Justify your suggestions.
questions.answer:
**Production**
- Replace the Bunsen burner and water bath with a **heating mantle (or electric hot plate)**: methanol and the other organic substances are volatile and flammable, so removing the naked flame reduces the risk of fire.
- Heat the mixture **under reflux** with a condenser fitted to the flask instead of moving the flask in and out of the bath. The volatile reactants and product are continuously condensed and returned to the flask, so they do not escape, the mixture can be kept hot for a long time, and the forward reaction continues.
- Heat for **several hours** (not 10 minutes): esterification is slow and reversible, so a longer time at the higher temperature (higher kinetic energy, more successful collisions) is needed to approach equilibrium and increase the yield. Add **boiling chips** so that the mixture boils smoothly and does not superheat during the long heating.

**Extraction**
- After neutralising the remaining acids (salicylic and sulfuric) with sodium carbonate, **wash the organic layer several times with water** in the separating funnel to dissolve and remove remaining water-soluble impurities (sulfuric acid, methanol, salicylic acid salts), improving purity.
- Add an anhydrous **drying agent** (e.g. anhydrous $\text{MgSO}_4$) to the separated organic layer to remove remaining water.
- **Distil** the dried product and collect the fraction at the boiling point of methyl salicylate to purify it from other organic compounds.

questions.question: The graph shows the boiling points of two homologous series of straight-chained organic compounds, aldehydes and primary alcohols, plotted against molar mass. Series X (crosses) has the higher boiling points (from about $65\ ^\circ\text{C}$ at $32\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$ to about $157\ ^\circ\text{C}$ at $102\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$) and series W (dots) has lower boiling points (from about $-19\ ^\circ\text{C}$ at $30\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$ to about $131\ ^\circ\text{C}$ at $100\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$). Identify the data X and W as either aldehydes or alcohols.
questions.answer: X is the alcohols and W is the aldehydes. Alcohols form hydrogen bonds, so they have higher boiling points than aldehydes of similar molar mass.

questions.question: The graph shows the boiling points of two homologous series of straight-chained organic compounds, aldehydes and primary alcohols, plotted against molar mass. Series X (crosses) has the higher boiling points (from about $65\ ^\circ\text{C}$ at $32\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$ to about $157\ ^\circ\text{C}$ at $102\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$) and series W (dots) has lower boiling points (from about $-19\ ^\circ\text{C}$ at $30\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$ to about $131\ ^\circ\text{C}$ at $100\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$). (Series X is the alcohols and series W is the aldehydes.) Explain the trends in the data provided.
questions.answer:
**Trend 1: alcohols have higher boiling points than aldehydes of similar molar mass.** Alcohol molecules contain an $\text{O-H}$ group and form hydrogen bonds with each other (as well as dipole-dipole and dispersion forces), whereas aldehydes (with a $\text{C=O}$ group but no $\text{O-H}$) have only dipole-dipole and dispersion forces. Hydrogen bonds are stronger than dipole-dipole forces, so more energy is needed to overcome the intermolecular forces in alcohols, giving a higher boiling point.

**Trend 2: the boiling points of both series increase with molar mass.** A longer carbon chain means more electrons and a larger surface area, so stronger dispersion forces (greater instantaneous induced dipoles) between molecules. More energy is needed to separate the molecules, so the boiling point increases.

**Trend 3: the difference in boiling point between alcohols and aldehydes decreases as molar mass increases** (about $80\ ^\circ\text{C}$ for the smallest pair, about $25\ ^\circ\text{C}$ for the largest). As the chain gets longer, the dispersion forces make an increasingly large contribution to the total intermolecular forces, while the contribution of hydrogen bonding in the alcohols (one $\text{O-H}$ per molecule) becomes relatively smaller, so the difference caused by the hydrogen bonding decreases.

questions.question:
The flowchart shows reactions of six organic compounds A to F. Compound A has molecular formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$.

- A reacts with dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to give B and C.
- B does not react with $\text{H}^+/\text{KMnO}_4$.
- C reacts with $\text{H}^+/\text{KMnO}_4$ to give F.
- A reacts with HBr to give D and E.
- D reacts with NaOH/heat to give C.

Draw the structural formulae and state the IUPAC names of compounds A to F, justifying your structures with reference to the information provided in the flow chart.
questions.answer:
**Set 1 (school's main answer)**

| Compound | Name and condensed structure | Justification |
|---|---|---|
| A | 2-methylbut-1-ene, $\text{CH}_2{=}\text{C(CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ | $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$ is an unsaturated (alkene) hydrocarbon; it reacts with dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ (hydration) and HBr (addition). B is a tertiary alcohol, which needs the double bond to be on a carbon that also carries the branch (methyl group). |
| B | 2-methylbutan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{C(OH)(CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ | Hydration product that does not oxidise with acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$, so it is the tertiary alcohol (main product). |
| C | 2-methylbutan-1-ol, $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ | The other hydration product; it is oxidised by $\text{H}^+/\text{KMnO}_4$, so it is a primary alcohol (the minor product, OH on the end carbon). |
| D | 1-bromo-2-methylbutane, $\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ | Addition of HBr to A gives D and E. Substitution of D with NaOH/heat gives C (2-methylbutan-1-ol), so the Br of D is on carbon 1 (the Br is replaced by OH). |
| E | 2-bromo-2-methylbutane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CBr(CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ | The other (major) product of the addition of HBr to A. |
| F | 2-methylbutanoic acid, $\text{HOOC-CH(CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ | C is a primary alcohol, so oxidation with $\text{H}^+/\text{KMnO}_4$ gives the carboxylic acid. |

**Set 2 (also accepted by the school):** A = 2-methylbut-2-ene; B = 2-methylbutan-2-ol (tertiary); C = 3-methylbutan-2-ol (secondary alcohol, minor hydration product); D = 2-bromo-3-methylbutane (substitution with NaOH gives C); E = 2-bromo-2-methylbutane; F = 3-methylbutan-2-one (oxidation of a secondary alcohol gives a ketone). The full structural formulae for both sets are shown in the images.

questions.question:
A bottle is labelled $\text{C}_7\text{H}_{14}\text{O}_2$. A sample was analysed by infrared spectroscopy, $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR and $^1\text{H}$ NMR. The spectra are shown (infrared with strong peaks at about $2981\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ and $1733\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ and no broad absorption above $2500\ \text{cm}^{-1}$; $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR peaks at about 173, 67, 37, 22, 19 and 14 ppm).

Data from the $^1\text{H}$ NMR spectrum:

| Chemical shift (ppm) | Relative peak area | Splitting pattern |
|---|---|---|
| 5.011 | 1 | septet (7) |
| 2.238 | 2 | triplet (3) |
| 1.645 | 2 | sextet (6) |
| 1.229 | 6 | doublet (2) |
| 0.951 | 3 | triplet (3) |

$^1\text{H}$ NMR chemical shift data: R-$\text{CH}_3$ 0.7-1.3; R-$\text{CH}_2$-R 1.2-1.5; R-$\text{CHR}_2$ 1.5-2.0; $\text{H}_3\text{C-CO-}$ (aldehydes, ketones, esters) 2.0-2.5; -CH-CO- 2.1-2.6; -CH-O- (alcohols or esters) 3.3-5.1; R-OH 1-6; R-CHO 9.4-10.0; R-COOH 9.0-13.0.

Draw a structural formula for the unknown compound that is consistent with all the information provided and justify your answer with reference to the information provided. (The IUPAC name is not required.)
questions.answer:
**Structure:** propan-2-yl butanoate (isopropyl butanoate), $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{C(=O)OCH(CH}_3)_2$ (an ester; $\text{C}_7\text{H}_{14}\text{O}_2$).

**Infrared:** the strong peak at about $1733\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ is a $\text{C=O}$ bond and the strong peak at about $2981\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ is $\text{C-H}$. There is no broad peak at $3230$ to $3550\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ (no alcohol $\text{O-H}$) and no very broad peak at $2500$ to $3000\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ (no carboxylic acid), so the compound is a carbonyl compound that is not an acid or alcohol; with two oxygens, an ester.

**$^{13}\text{C}$ NMR:** there are 7 carbons but 6 carbon environments, so two carbons are equivalent by symmetry (the two $\text{CH}_3$ groups on the same carbon). The peak at about 173 ppm is an ester $\text{C=O}$ carbon (160 to 185 ppm); the peak at about 67 ppm is a carbon singly bonded to oxygen ($\text{C-O}$, 50 to 90 ppm); the peak at about 37 ppm is the carbon next to the carbonyl (20 to 50 ppm); the remaining peaks at about 22, 19 and 14 ppm are alkyl carbons (5 to 40 ppm).

**$^1\text{H}$ NMR:** there are five hydrogen environments and the peak areas (1:2:2:6:3, total 14) match the 14 hydrogens in the formula.
- $5.011$ ppm, area 1, septet: one H with 6 neighbouring H ($n+1=7$), i.e. $-\text{CH(CH}_3)_2$; the high shift shows it is next to the ester oxygen ($-\text{CH-O-}$, 3.3 to 5.1 ppm).
- $2.238$ ppm, area 2, triplet: a $\text{CH}_2$ with 2 neighbouring H ($n+1=3$) next to the carbonyl ($-\text{CH}_2-\text{CO-}$, 2.1 to 2.6 ppm).
- $1.645$ ppm, area 2, sextet: a $\text{CH}_2$ with 5 neighbouring H (the $\text{CH}_2$ and $\text{CH}_3$), i.e. $\text{R-CH}_2-\text{R}$, in the middle of the butanoyl chain.
- $1.229$ ppm, area 6, doublet: two equivalent $\text{CH}_3$ groups, each with 1 neighbouring H ($n+1=2$), the $\text{CH}_3$ groups of the isopropyl group.
- $0.951$ ppm, area 3, triplet: a terminal $\text{CH}_3$ with 2 neighbouring H, $\text{R-CH}_3$.

All data are consistent with $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH(CH}_3)_2$ (the marking guide also accepts a correct isomer).
